title: The Young Astronomer of Samarkand
summary: A young apprentice at the historical Samarkand observatory measures star positions night after night, and his careful, patient work helps catch an error in an important star catalog.
poll: Checking your work carefully, over and over, is more important than working fast.

versions.title: The Young Astronomer
versions.text:
Tariq is a boy. He lives in an old city. It is Samarkand.

Long ago, a king built a tall tower. It is an observatory. Men go up it at night. They look at stars.

Tariq helps the men. He is young. He has one job. He must see where a star sits. He must measure it. Then he writes it down. He checks it two times. He is careful.

The men keep a big star book. It has numbers for many stars.

One night, Tariq looks at an old record. The old number is not the same. He checks it again. It still is not the same.

Tariq feels scared. But he tells the head man.

The head man checks it. Tariq is right! There is a mistake.

The men fix it. The star book is right now.

versions.title: The Young Astronomer
versions.text:
Tariq is a young boy. He lives in the old, busy city of Samarkand. He loves watching the night sky.

Long ago, a wise king named Ulugh Beg built a tall tower. People call it an observatory. The men who work there climb its long stairs every clear night. They study the stars above the sleeping city.

Tariq helps these men. He is one of the youngest helpers there. He has one job that matters most. He must measure exactly where each star sits, using a huge pointed tool. Then he writes every number down in a thick book. He checks each number two times, because he wants to be very careful.

The men are building a big star book. It is full of careful numbers for many stars. One day, other men in faraway cities will use this same book.

One quiet night, Tariq looks closely at an old record. The old number does not match the fresh number he just measured. He checks both numbers again, slowly and patiently. They still do not match, no matter how many times he looks.

Tariq feels nervous about what he found. Still, he walks over to tell the head man.

The head man checks the numbers carefully, step by step. Tariq is right! There is a small mistake hidden inside the great star book.

The men fix the mistake together, before the sun comes up. Thanks to careful young Tariq, the great star book is finally right.

versions.title: The Young Astronomer of Samarkand
versions.text:
Long ago, in old Samarkand, a wise ruler named Ulugh Beg built a tall, round observatory. Astronomers climbed its stairs each night. They studied the stars above the city.

Tariq was one of the youngest helpers there. Each evening he climbed the stairs beside the older men. He carried ink and paper to help them in the dark.

Tariq's job was simple to describe, but hard to do well. He had to measure exactly where a star sat in the sky. He used a huge curved instrument fixed to the wall. He wrote every number in a book. Then he checked it twice, slowly and patiently, before moving to the next star's position.

The astronomers were building a big star catalog. It was a careful list of star positions. Men in other cities would use this catalog to find their way at night.

One quiet night, Tariq noticed something odd. An old record for one star did not match his fresh measurement. He checked both numbers again, slowly. They still did not match.

Tariq felt a flash of fear. Who was he to question the head astronomer's math? Still, he found his courage and brought his notes over.

The head astronomer checked the calculation step by step. To his surprise, Tariq was right: a small error had crept into the great catalog.

The men fixed the mistake before dawn. Because one patient apprentice kept careful watch, the star catalog became more accurate for everyone.

versions.text:
Long ago, in Samarkand, a scholarly ruler named Ulugh Beg built a magnificent round observatory on a hill overlooking the city's crowded rooftops. Night after night, teams of astronomers climbed its long stone stairways. They made careful observations of the stars filling the clear desert sky above them.

Tariq was among the youngest apprentices at this busy, respected observatory. He was eager to prove that his own careful attention could rival that of astronomers twice his age. Each evening he climbed the worn stone stairs beside the older scholars, carrying ink, paper, and a small lantern to help everyone see once the sun had set.

Tariq's job was simple to describe, though demanding to perform well night after night without a single lapse. He had to measure exactly where each star appeared in the sky, using a large curved instrument built into the thick stone wall. He recorded every number in a heavy logbook and checked each figure twice, slowly and patiently, before measuring the next star's precise position.

The astronomers were compiling a large star catalog, a careful list of star positions calculated and rechecked over many patient years. Scholars in distant cities would rely on this catalog to navigate and to study the slow movements of the heavens.

One quiet night, while comparing a column of old and new figures, Tariq noticed something unusual. An old record for one star simply failed to match the fresh measurement he had just taken with his own hands. He checked both numbers again, slowly, tracing each figure with his finger. They still stubbornly refused to agree.

A flicker of fear rose in Tariq's chest at what his checking had uncovered. Who was he, a young apprentice barely a year into his training, to question a calculation made by the head astronomer himself? Still, he gathered his courage and carried his notes to the head astronomer's desk.

The head astronomer studied the disputed calculation with great care, checking it step by patient step against Tariq's own measurements from earlier nights. To nearly everyone's surprise, Tariq turned out to be entirely correct: a small error had crept quietly into the great catalog, unnoticed for months by eyes far more experienced than his own.

Working together long into the night, the team corrected the mistake before the first light of dawn appeared over the hills. Because of one determined apprentice's careful, precise observation, the star catalog became measurably more accurate for every scholar who would depend on its numbers.

Still, he gathered his courage and carried his careful notes across the room to the head astronomer's desk.

keyWords.definition: a bright point of light you see in the night sky
keyWords.example: I counted ten stars from my window last night.

keyWords.definition: a special building people use to study the sky and stars
keyWords.example: Our class visited an observatory to look through a big telescope.

keyWords.definition: to find out the exact size, amount, or position of something
keyWords.example: The nurse used a tool to measure my height.

keyWords.definition: paying close attention so you do not make a mistake
keyWords.example: Be careful when you carry a full glass of water.

keyWords.definition: to write down information so you can look at it later
keyWords.example: The scientist asked her helper to record the temperature every hour.

questions.stem: What is this story mostly about?
options: A ruler who teaches a boy to ride a horse
A boy who gets lost on the way to school
A boy who helps measure stars and finds a mistake
A boy who builds a new observatory by himself
questions.why: The story follows Tariq as he measures stars night after night and finds a mistake in the star book.

wrong.A: The story does not talk about horses.
wrong.B: Tariq is not lost on the way to school.
wrong.D: Ulugh Beg built the observatory, not Tariq.

questions.stem: Who built the tall tower in the story?
options: A king
Tariq
The head man
A traveling merchant
questions.why: The story says a king built the tall tower, which is the observatory.

wrong.B: Tariq is a young helper, not the builder.
wrong.C: The head man works there but did not build it.
wrong.D: No merchant is mentioned in the story.

questions.stem: What is Tariq's main job at the observatory?
options: To sell books in the city market
To measure stars and write down the numbers
To cook food for the men who work there
To clean the stairs every morning before work
questions.why: The story says Tariq must measure where a star sits and write the number in a book.

wrong.A: Tariq does not sell books.
wrong.D: Cleaning stairs is not Tariq's job in the story.

questions.stem: In the story, when Tariq checks a number two times, he is being —
options: lost
angry
lazy
careful
questions.why: The story says Tariq checks each number two times because he wants to be careful.

wrong.A: Tariq is not lost; he knows exactly what he is doing.
wrong.B: The story does not say Tariq is angry.
wrong.C: Checking twice is the opposite of lazy.

questions.stem: What happens right after Tariq finds that two numbers do not match?
options: He goes home for the night
He checks both numbers again
He throws the book away
He asks a merchant for help
questions.why: The story says Tariq checks both numbers again after noticing they do not match.

wrong.A: Tariq does not go home; he keeps checking.
wrong.C: Tariq does not throw the book away.
wrong.D: Tariq tells the head man, not a merchant.

questions.stem: Why does Tariq decide to tell the head man about the two numbers?
options: Because the head man asked him to come and explain the problem
Because he wants a new job in the factory office next month
Because he thinks the mistake matters, even though he is scared
Because he wants to stop working at the yard and go home
questions.why: The story says Tariq feels scared but still tells the head man, showing he thinks it matters.

wrong.A: The head man did not call Tariq over.
wrong.B: The story does not say Tariq wants a new job.
wrong.D: Tariq keeps working; he does not want to stop.

questions.stem: What can you tell about Tariq from how carefully he checks his numbers?
options: He does not know how to count
He wants his work to be correct
He does not care about his work
He is too scared to work at all
questions.why: Checking numbers two times shows Tariq wants his measurements to be right.

wrong.A: Tariq clearly knows how to count and measure.
wrong.C: Checking carefully shows he does care.
wrong.D: Tariq keeps working even when he feels nervous.

questions.stem: Why does the story end with the men fixing the star book?
options: To show that stars do not matter to anyone at all
To show that the star book was never used again by the men
To show that the king was angry at Tariq for his work
To show that Tariq's careful work made a real difference
questions.why: The ending shows that Tariq's careful checking led to an important fix in the star book.

wrong.A: The whole story shows that stars matter a great deal.
wrong.B: The story says the star book will help many people, so it is still used.
wrong.C: The king is not shown as angry in the story.

LOW.prompt: Do you think Tariq was right to tell the head man about the mistake, even though he was scared? Use at least two facts from the story.
checklist: I clearly said what I think.
I used at least two facts from the story.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.

MID.prompt: Explain how Tariq's patient, careful habits helped him catch the error in the star catalog. Use at least two details from the story.
checklist: I explained how Tariq's habits led to catching the error.
I used at least two details from the story.

MID.modelAnswer: Tariq's patient, careful habits are the reason he caught the error. Every night, he measured each star's position with the instrument and checked each number twice before moving on. Because he was so used to checking carefully, he noticed right away when an old record did not match his new measurement. Instead of ignoring the strange numbers, he calculated them again slowly and then brought his notes to the head astronomer, which led to the mistake being fixed.

HIGH.prompt: The poll says checking your work carefully, over and over, matters more than working fast. Do you agree or disagree? Support your argument with evidence from the story about Tariq's observations.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the poll statement.
I supported my position with specific evidence from the story.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that careful, repeated checking matters more than working fast. In the story, Tariq's habit of checking every measurement twice is exactly what let him notice that an old record did not match his new observation; if he had rushed, he likely would have missed the discrepancy entirely. His precise, patient approach also gave him enough confidence in his own numbers to bring the problem to the head astronomer, even though doing so felt risky for a young apprentice. Someone might argue that working quickly lets astronomers measure more stars overall, but a catalog full of fast, uncorrected errors would be far less useful to future scholars than a smaller, precise one they can actually trust.
